strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question for human-in-the-loop NLP: how collaboration settings affect theme discovery and annotation quality. Its attention to qualitative researchers’ workflows gives the evaluation clear practical motivation.
Comparing topic modeling, relational inference, and an LLM on a common corpus provides useful breadth. Keeping initial partitions fixed within each system is a sensible experimental control.

The evaluation combines assignment overlap, semantic similarity, human correctness judgments, and participant feedback. The 1,200 double-annotated document-theme pairs with adjudication provide substantive human evidence, and reporting Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.632 makes its reliability assessable.

The manuscript clearly explains the selected systems and includes useful implementation information, prompt templates, and an interview script. Its acknowledgment of dataset and evaluation limitations is welcome.
weaknesses: The experimental contrast does not isolate collaboration timing. Section 4 compares three-person synchronous groups with individual coders, without the subsequent consolidation used to define asynchronous collaboration earlier in the paper. Group size, available perspectives, and potentially effort therefore change together. Participant allocation, reuse, ordering, and session durations are insufficiently documented. The conclusions should be narrowed to this specific individual-versus-group comparison, or supported by comparable team workflows.

The statistical significance claims are inadequately justified. Each system has only two synchronous and three individual codebooks, yet Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without specifying sampling units, sample sizes, or degrees of freedom. Theme matches are nested within sessions, and pairwise comparisons reuse codebooks; treating these observations as independent would constitute pseudoreplication. Session-level results and an analysis accounting for these dependencies are necessary to establish the central effects.

The proposed framework needs stronger validation as a measure of codebook quality. Maximum-similarity matching leaves directionality, weighting, and handling of many-to-one matches unclear, while theme counts and size distributions are unreported. These choices can materially affect consistency scores. Table 1’s centroid similarities of 0.94–0.98 despite much lower document overlap also warrant calibration against a baseline or human judgments of theme equivalence.

The correctness evaluation is not sufficiently specified. Section 5 describes judgments of document-theme assignments, but Figure 4 reports an undefined F1 score without explaining its classes, aggregation, or uncertainty. The claimed asynchronous advantage for topic modeling is inconsistent with the plotted curves: they coincide for the full sample and favor synchronous coding at intermediate cutoffs. Treatment of unassigned documents is also unclear, despite invalid LLM labels affecting 0.7%–16.1% of documents across sessions.

The broader conclusions about LLM reliability and expense exceed the evidence from one Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct implementation. One supplied prompt confuses qualitative codes with programming concepts such as object classes and code functionality, and the selected template for each session is not identified. The reported 24 GPU-hours per job lacks comparable resource accounting for the other systems. These observations support conclusions about the tested configuration, not LLM-based coding generally.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite Section 9’s assertion that all necessary details are provided. Missing information includes the exact sentence-embedding checkpoint, LLM decoding settings, prompt-selection sample sizes, final codebooks, and sufficient evaluation details to reconstruct the reported statistics. Annotation outputs and analysis code are promised rather than supplied through an identifiable artifact.

The interview findings are useful exploratory observations, but Appendix C acknowledges missing interviews without reporting completion counts or their distribution across conditions. The analysis procedure and participant-level support for the reported themes are also absent. Together with the experimental and statistical issues above, these gaps prevent a clear Findings recommendation; the decisive concerns are evidential support and reproducibility.
